Width and depth: does a bigger network predict better? {#part-i} ## Motivation A logistic item response model is a very small neural network. The Rasch model takes a person, looks up one number for them ($\theta_p$), takes an item, looks up one number for it ($d_i$, the negative of the difficulty), adds the two, and passes the sum through a sigmoid. In PyTorch terms that is two `nn.Embedding` layers and no hidden layer at all. The 2PL adds a second item lookup, the slope $a_i$, and multiplies before it adds. Once the models are written this way, a question that is awkward to pose in the psychometric idiom becomes the obvious next step: what happens when the network is made wider (more latent dimensions) or deeper (a multilayer perceptron between the embeddings and the response)? Does a neural network predict item responses better than the 2PL? The question is not new. Variational IRT [@wu2020variational] and the recommender-systems literature [@koren2009matrix; @he2017ncf] both treat person-by-item data as a matrix to be factorised and have explored exactly these widenings. What is missing is a comparison on an honest footing: the same held-out cells, the same prior on persons, the same scoring rule, across enough real tables of different kinds to see where a wider network helps and where it does not. That is the contribution here. We build the classical models in PyTorch, confirm that they recover what `mirt` [@chalmers2012mirt] recovers, widen and deepen them, and score every model on held-out responses from 24 IRW tables with the InterModel Vigorish [IMV, @domingue2024imv], which puts every gain on the scale of a bet. Two flexible one-dimensional models from `mirt`, the monotonic polynomial [@falk2016monotonic] and the logistic positive exponent [@samejima2000lpe], join the comparison, because they make the opposite move from the networks: they change the *shape* of the item curve while keeping a single dimension. The short version of the answer is that on a test built to measure one thing, nothing beats the 2PL; where a network wins, the win is a second dimension, and a two-dimensional MIRT finds it as well as a deeper network does. We then put that result to a harder test, applying a selection rule to the whole warehouse rather than a judgment to 24 tables, and fitting the 2PL against a two-dimensional MIRT on all 242 tables that qualify. The median table gains nothing; the mean gain, +0.0025, matches the published benchmark and is carried almost entirely by a seventh of the corpus. Those tables turn out to have something specific in common, and it is not a second trait --- it is reverse-keyed items that were never recoded. All of that holds at the sizes we fit here: tables are capped at 5,000 respondents and 116 items, and scale is the one advantage a wider network is supposed to have, so the null is a null at this scale. That is Part I. One of the comparisons also turned up an estimator effect, a small but consistent gap between the same 2PL fit in torch and in `mirt`, and Part II takes it apart: the estimator explains the gap, and fixing the scale of the person parameters does not. ## Data and methods ### Dataset selection We wanted tables that would spread across the kinds of structure a wider network might find, rather than a random sample of the warehouse. The 24 tables fall into five groups, fixed in `nn_irt_helpers.py`: - **Achievement and ability tests** built to measure one thing (a Brazilian medical residency exam, an ENCCEJA Portuguese form, a Dutch listening test, a general intelligence measure, two vocabulary and ability samples). - **Knowledge tests with heterogeneous content** (two COVID-19 knowledge scales, a financial literacy test, the Author Recognition Test), where the items range over topics and a single dimension is a convenience rather than a design. - **Tests with a documented multidimensional structure** (the ECPE grammar test with its three-attribute Q-matrix, a mental-rotation test, a medical licensing exam). - **Personality and clinical inventories** that mix several syndromes or facets in one table (the Woodworth Psychoneurotic Inventory, the NPI, the Taylor Manifest Anxiety scale, the Eysenck EPI, the MCMI, and four more). - **Developmental screeners** (the ASQ and Denver items from the D-score project), which span motor, language and social domains and are age-adaptive, so each child answers only a slice of the items. All are dense and dichotomous. The response values are checked at fetch time rather than trusted from metadata; one candidate, `vocabulary_iq`, turned out to be polytomous despite its metadata and was dropped (and the metadata corrected upstream); two further candidates, `encceja_2025_em_cn` and `mgkt_options`, were dropped because their full exports fail to load, so the final 24 is a design choice filtered by what we could read. Tables with more than 5,000 respondents or 116 items are subsampled to those caps with a fixed seed, so that every fit on the page stays small enough to run on a laptop. This selection is deliberate and it is *not* a sample: these 24 tables were picked to span kinds of structure, which makes them good for showing where gains come from and bad for estimating how often gains occur. Sizes are after subsampling. ### Held-out cells, not held-out people Every model here has a parameter per person. A model cannot predict a person it has never seen, so the usual split by rows (train on some people, test on others) is not available. We hold out **cells** instead: 20% of each person's responses, chosen at random, are hidden during training and predicted afterwards. Every person and every item stays in the training set. The same mask is used by every model, including the `mirt` fits, which see the held-out cells as missing. This is the cross-validation design of the IMV paper, and it is the only one that makes sense when persons are parameters. ### The models, written as networks The four model classes below are the whole of the modelling code. Each takes a batch of person indices and item indices and returns a logit. | Model | Person lookup | Item lookup | Combine | Parameters | On the residency exam | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Rasch | $\theta_p$ (1 number) | $d_i$ (1 number) | $\theta_p + d_i$ | $N + J$ | 3,339 | | 2PL | $\theta_p$ (1) | $a_i, d_i$ (2) | $a_i\theta_p + d_i$ | $N + 2J$ | 3,455 | | MIRT, $k$ dims | $\boldsymbol\theta_p$ ($k$) | $\mathbf a_i$ ($k$), $d_i$ | $\mathbf a_i \cdot \boldsymbol\theta_p + d_i$ | $kN + (k+1)J$ | 6,794 | | Multilayer perceptron (MLP), $k$ dims | $\boldsymbol\theta_p$ ($k$) | $\mathbf v_i$ ($k$) | $\mathrm{MLP}([\boldsymbol\theta_p, \mathbf v_i])$ | $kN + kJ + $ decoder | 6,775 (small), 11,223 (large) | Here $N$ is the number of persons and $J$ the number of items, and the residency exam column counts parameters for the first table on the page (3,223 persons, 116 items, $k = 2$). The decoder of the small MLP has 97 weights and that of the large one 4,545, so even the large network is mostly embeddings: the step from one dimension to two more than doubles the parameter count, and depth adds comparatively little on top. The models are written in slope-intercept form, $a_i\theta_p + d_i$, as `mirt` writes them, rather than the textbook $a_i(\theta_p - b_i)$. This is not cosmetic. In the textbook form the gradient for $b_i$ is scaled by $a_i$, so the difficulties of weak items barely move during training, and a slope kept positive by an exponential cannot fit an item keyed against the trait, which several of the inventories below contain. The slope here is signed and unconstrained. The MIRT model is the compensatory multidimensional 2PL [@reckase2009mirt]: $k$-dimensional person and item embeddings combined by a dot product, which is also a rank-$k$ factorisation of the logit matrix. With $k=1$ it is the 2PL; we use $k=2$. The multilayer perceptron, the plain feed-forward neural network and the thing most people mean by "a neural net", concatenates the two embeddings and passes them through one or more hidden layers of rectified linear units before a final linear layer produces the logit. The interaction between person and item is then no longer constrained to be a dot product; this is the shape used in neural collaborative filtering [@he2017ncf]. We fit two sizes, both on $k=2$ embeddings: a small one with a single hidden layer of 16 units, and a large one with two hidden layers of 64, so that depth is the only thing that changes between them. ### Estimation The PyTorch models are fit by minibatch gradient descent (Adam) on the mean negative log-likelihood plus a $N(0,1)$ prior on $\theta_p$, which makes each fit a maximum a posteriori estimate rather than joint maximum likelihood (the section that follows builds this up line by line). The prior is the only thing identifying the scale of $\theta$ on this page, and it is used that way throughout: everything in Part I is the MAP fit. The obvious alternative is to standardise $\theta$ to mean zero and SD one inside the model, which fixes the scale exactly rather than softly; [Part II](#constraining-the-scale) fits every model both ways and reports what that costs, which is why the prior is what we use here. Each model is trained for up to 30 epochs and the epoch with the lowest held-out loss is reported. That is early stopping with the held-out set doing double duty as a validation set; a production comparison would carve out a third split, and we return to what this choice costs in the results. The `mirt` models are fit offline by marginal maximum likelihood [@bock1981marginal] on the same training cells, in `nn_irt_mirt_compute.R`, and each held-out cell is predicted by its posterior-predictive probability: the item curve integrated over the person's posterior on a quadrature grid. Three models are fit this way: the 2PL again, as the marginal-likelihood anchor for the PyTorch 2PL; the monotonic polynomial model, whose item curve is a flexible monotone function rather than a logistic; and the logistic positive exponent (LPE) model, whose item curve is asymmetric. ### Scoring Every model is scored on the same held-out cells by log-loss and by the IMV against the PyTorch 2PL. The IMV converts a log-loss improvement into a bet: if model 0 predicts held-out responses as well as a coin with bias $w_0$ and model 1 as well as a coin with bias $w_1$, the IMV is $(w_1 - w_0)/w_0$, the relative gain in the bettor's edge. The [IMV vignette](imv.qmd) has the derivation and the R package. In Python we use the [`imvpy`](https://github.com/intermodelvigorish/imvpy) package, whose `vanilla_imv` takes the baseline probabilities, the enhanced probabilities and the outcomes, in that order. The definition is short enough to write out, and the helper module does so; the two agree on the first table's held-out cells to the fourth decimal, the residual being how extreme probabilities are clipped. ::: {#imv-check .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} import inspect print(inspect.getsource(imv)) _te = data["borges_brazil_residency_2024_cbt"] _te = _te[_te.test] _y, _p0 = _te.resp.values, np.full(len(_te), _te.resp.mean()) _p1 = np.clip(_p0 + 0.2 * (_y - 0.5), 0.05, 0.95) # a deliberately better forecast print(f"helper imv {imv(_y, _p0, _p1):.5f}") print(f"imvpy {vanilla_imv(_p0, _p1, _y):.5f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` def imv(y: np.ndarray, p0: np.ndarray, p1: np.ndarray) -> float: """InterModel Vigorish of model 1 over model 0 on held-out cells.""" w0 = equivalent_coin(log_loss(y, p0)) w1 = equivalent_coin(log_loss(y, p1)) return (w1 - w0) / w0 helper imv 0.41904 imvpy 0.41904 ``` ::: ::: ## Building the network, step by step Before the comparison, we write the 2PL as a network from nothing but `torch`, on one table, so that each piece can be seen. The helper module used later is this code with bookkeeping added. ### 1. Long data is already the right shape A neural network consumes one training example at a time, and an item response is one example: a person index, an item index, a 0/1 outcome. Nothing has to be reshaped to a wide matrix; IRW's long format is the network's native input. Three integer-coded columns become three tensors. ::: {#e7d6c43b .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} d = data["borges_brazil_residency_2024_cbt"] train = d[~d.test] P = torch.tensor(train.pid.values) # person index, 0..n_persons-1 I = torch.tensor(train.iid.values) # item index, 0..n_items-1 Y = torch.tensor(train.resp.values, dtype=torch.float32) # 0/1 response n_p, n_i = int(d.pid.max() + 1), int(d.iid.max() + 1) P[:5], I[:5], Y[:5], (n_p, n_i) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (tensor([1946, 506, 1335, 1109, 3172]), tensor([0, 0, 0, 0, 0]), tensor([0., 0., 0., 0., 0.]), (3223, 116)) ``` ::: ::: ### 2. An embedding is a lookup table of parameters `nn.Embedding(n, k)` is an $n \times k$ table of trainable numbers. Indexing it with a tensor of integers returns the matching rows. A person embedding of width 1 is a column of $\theta_p$; an item embedding of width 1 is a column of $d_i$. There is no "input layer" in the usual sense: the index *is* the input. ::: {#a6b3e693 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} import torch.nn as nn theta = nn.Embedding(n_p, 1) # one number per person theta.weight.shape, theta(P[:3]) # rows for the first three training cells ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` (torch.Size([3223, 1]), tensor([[-0.6911], [ 1.6743], [ 0.2542]], grad_fn=)) ``` ::: ::: ### 3. The forward pass is the item response function For the 2PL the logit is $a_i \theta_p + d_i$: look up three numbers and combine them. A `Module` packages the lookups and the combination, and its `forward` method is the item response function on the logit scale. The sigmoid that turns a logit into a probability is folded into the loss below, which is numerically safer than applying it here. ::: {#2df3dd79 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} class TwoPLNet(nn.Module): def __init__(self, n_persons, n_items): super().__init__() self.theta = nn.Embedding(n_persons, 1) # person ability self.a = nn.Embedding(n_items, 1) # item slope (signed) self.d = nn.Embedding(n_items, 1) # item intercept (= -a * difficulty) nn.init.normal_(self.theta.weight, std=0.1) nn.init.ones_(self.a.weight) nn.init.zeros_(self.d.weight) def forward(self, p, i): return (self.a(i) * self.theta(p) + self.d(i)).squeeze(-1) net = TwoPLNet(n_p, n_i) logits = net(P[:5], I[:5]) logits, torch.sigmoid(logits) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` (tensor([-0.0286, 0.0744, 0.1041, -0.0284, 0.0477], grad_fn=), tensor([0.4928, 0.5186, 0.5260, 0.4929, 0.5119], grad_fn=)) ``` ::: ::: At initialisation every item has slope 1 and intercept 0 and every person is near 0, so every probability is about one half. ### 4. The loss is the negative log-likelihood `BCEWithLogitsLoss` is $-\frac{1}{n}\sum_c \big[y_c \log p_c + (1-y_c)\log(1-p_c)\big]$ with $p_c = \sigma(\text{logit}_c)$: the mean negative log-likelihood of a Bernoulli model, which is exactly the quantity an IRT package maximises. Before training it is $\log 2 \approx 0.693$, the log-loss of a fair coin. ::: {#1a159bff .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} loss_fn = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss() loss_fn(net(P, I), Y).item() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` 0.6942257285118103 ``` ::: ::: ### 5. A prior on persons, but not on items Persons and items are both parameters here, but they are not in the same position. Each item is answered by thousands of persons, so its slope and intercept are pinned down by the data and need no help. Each person answers a dozen to a hundred items, and there is a new $\theta_p$ for every person added to the sample, so the person parameters never stop multiplying. Fitting a free $\theta_p$ for every person by maximum likelihood is joint maximum likelihood, which is inconsistent as the number of persons grows [@haberman1977maximum] and runs away for perfect scores. IRT software avoids this by integrating $\theta$ out under a $N(0,1)$ prior, which is marginal maximum likelihood [@bock1981marginal]; the item parameters are left as free fixed effects, exactly as they are here. The network's equivalent is to add $\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_p \theta_p^2$ to the loss, scaled by $1/n$ to match the mean log-likelihood. That makes the fit a MAP estimate under the same normal prior, and it is a single line. Nothing here puts a prior on the item slopes, and the networks do not need one for the comparison. ::: {#02e32034 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} def objective(net, p, i, y, n=len(train)): nll = loss_fn(net(p, i), y) prior = 0.5 * (net.theta(p) ** 2).sum() / n # N(0,1) prior on theta return nll + prior ``` ::: (The helper module spreads the prior over each person's responses so that it is unbiased in a minibatch; the idea is the same.) ### 6. The training loop Gradient descent on the objective, in minibatches, with Adam as the optimiser. Each pass over the training cells is an epoch. This is the whole algorithm; everything else is monitoring. ::: {#2b5a9434 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} torch.manual_seed(SEED) opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=0.02) n, batch = len(train), 4096 for epoch in range(10): perm = torch.randperm(n) for s in range(0, n, batch): j = perm[s:s + batch] opt.zero_grad() objective(net, P[j], I[j], Y[j]).backward() opt.step() with torch.no_grad(): print(f"epoch {epoch + 1:2d} train log-loss {loss_fn(net(P, I), Y).item():.4f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` epoch 1 train log-loss 0.5571 epoch 2 train log-loss 0.5430 epoch 3 train log-loss 0.5409 epoch 4 train log-loss 0.5402 epoch 5 train log-loss 0.5399 epoch 6 train log-loss 0.5398 epoch 7 train log-loss 0.5398 epoch 8 train log-loss 0.5397 epoch 9 train log-loss 0.5397 epoch 10 train log-loss 0.5397 ``` ::: ::: Ten epochs take a few seconds on a laptop CPU, and the training log-loss settles at the value the 2PL can reach on this table. Held-out predictions are the same forward pass on the held-out indices, through a sigmoid: ::: {#ae1fee07 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} test = d[d.test] with torch.no_grad(): p_test = torch.sigmoid(net(torch.tensor(test.pid.values), torch.tensor(test.iid.values))).numpy() log_loss(test.resp.values, p_test) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ``` 0.5479427278744378 ``` ::: ::: That is a complete item response model, fit by a neural-network toolkit, in about thirty lines. The Rasch model drops the slope. The multidimensional model makes the embeddings wider. The MLP replaces the dot product with hidden layers. All four live in the helper module with the same training loop (`fit`), which also records train and held-out loss per epoch. ## Results ### The network recovers what mirt recovers First, the Rasch and 2PL models from the helper module, trained with the same loop as above on the residency exam, each reported by its training and held-out log-loss after the final epoch. The 2PL's held-out loss is the number to carry forward: everything else on the page is scored against it. ::: {#fit-one .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Fit Rasch and 2PL on the residency exam"} rasch, h_rasch = fit(Rasch(n_p, n_i), d) twopl, h_2pl = fit(TwoPL(n_p, n_i), d) for name, h in (("Rasch", h_rasch), ("2PL", h_2pl)): last = h.iloc[-1] print(f"{name:6s} after {int(last.epoch)} epochs: " f"train log-loss {last.train:.4f}, held-out log-loss {last.test:.4f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rasch after 80 epochs: train log-loss 0.5495, held-out log-loss 0.5576 2PL after 80 epochs: train log-loss 0.5396, held-out log-loss 0.5478 ``` ::: ::: Does the network recover the item parameters? The offline `mirt` 2PL fit wrote its slopes and intercepts next to its predictions, so we can compare item by item. ::: {#cell-fig-recovery .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Item parameters: PyTorch against mirt"} ref = pd.read_csv("nn_irt_data/borges_brazil_residency_2024_cbt_mirt_2pl_items.csv", dtype={"item": str}) ref = ref.set_index("item").reindex(sorted(d["item"].unique())) fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4)) ax[0].scatter(ref.d, twopl.d.weight.detach().numpy().ravel(), s=12) ax[0].set(xlabel="mirt 2PL intercept $d$", ylabel="PyTorch 2PL intercept $d$") sd_theta = twopl.theta.weight.detach().numpy().std() ax[1].scatter(ref.a, twopl.a.weight.detach().numpy().ravel() * sd_theta, s=12) ax[1].set(xlabel="mirt 2PL slope $a$", ylabel=r"PyTorch 2PL slope $a \times \mathrm{sd}(\hat\theta)$") for a_ in ax: lo, hi = a_.get_xlim(); a_.plot([lo, hi], [lo, hi], "k--", lw=0.8) plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](nn_irt_files/figure-html/fig-recovery-output-1.png){#fig-recovery width=978 height=428} ::: ::: The intercepts agree to the dot. The slopes agree once the scale of $\theta$ is accounted for: `mirt` fixes the *population* variance of $\theta$ at one, while the network's point estimates are shrunk by the prior and have a smaller spread, so its raw slopes are proportionally larger. Multiplying them by the spread of $\hat\theta$ puts the two on the same footing. The remaining scatter is the difference between a point estimate for each person and integrating the person out, to which we return below. ### Wider networks overfit, and early stopping is the fix Now the models that are not classical IRT, still on the residency exam. Before looking, it helps to say what to expect. Training loss should fall in order of parameter count: a model with more freedom can always fit the cells it is shown at least as well as a model with less, so the Rasch curve should sit highest, the 2PL below it, and the three wider models below that. Held-out loss is a different matter. Extra parameters only help there if they capture something that generalises from a person's training cells to their held-out ones; if they do not, the model spends its freedom memorising the training cells, and held-out loss turns upward after an early minimum. ``` ::: ::: ### On tests built to measure one thing, nothing beats the 2PL Across the achievement and ability tests, the knowledge tests and two of the three exams with a documented multidimensional structure, the wider networks sit within about 0.01 IMV of the 2PL, and as often below it as above. For calibration, the IMV paper puts the gain from 1PL to 2PL on typical cognitive data at roughly the value of knowing someone's age when predicting chronic disease; the gains here are a fraction of that, and they go both ways. The ECPE grammar test is the instructive case. It has a known three-attribute Q-matrix, and a model built to find structure still predicts no better, because the attributes are too correlated to carry separate signal in held-out cells. Structure that is real in the design can be invisible in prediction. The one clear exception in this group is the FSIQ mental-rotation test, where every wider network gains about 0.03. We first read that as the test failing to be unidimensional in practice whatever it was built to measure. The sweep below says otherwise: 42% of its items take a negative 2PL slope, the highest share of any table named on this page, and the second dimension lines up with that split almost perfectly. The gain is scoring, not spatial ability. ### Where the networks win, a two-dimensional 2PL wins too The gains cluster in the personality and clinical inventories: about 0.03 on the ADQ anhedonia scale, 0.02 on the Eysenck EPI (three scales in one table), 0.008 on the Woodworth, with smaller gains on the Author Recognition Test and the GMI. Seven of the 24 tables show a gain above 0.005 and the other seventeen sit within noise of the 2PL, so the positive result rests on a minority of these tables; that is what one would expect if a second dimension is something an instrument has or lacks rather than a general property of item response data. In every one of these the MLPs match or trail the two-dimensional MIRT, and the large MLP is never reliably better than the small one. Once the embeddings are two-dimensional, a nonlinear decoder adds nothing on these data. Put differently: the signal a network can find in a person-by-item table of this kind is a second dimension, and an ordinary two-dimensional 2PL finds it. Depth is not where the signal is. What that second dimension *is* turns out to vary, and the sweep below separates two cases: the ADQ, the EPI and the mental-rotation test all carry reverse-keyed items, while the GMI and the Author Recognition Test gain with every slope positive. Keying explains most of the gains on this page, but not all of them. The Rasch row shows the same thing from the other side. Its large losses (0.11 on the NPI, 0.08 on the ADQ, 0.07 on the Denver screener) are tables where slopes differ sharply across items, including reverse-keyed items a Rasch model cannot fit at all. The step from one item parameter to two is worth more than every step after it. ### Flexible item curves do not add much The asymmetric LPE curve tracks the `mirt` 2PL to within 0.003 on every table, very slightly above it on average. The monotonic polynomial is the same on the tests and worse on several inventories (0.04 below on the NPI, 0.015 on the ADQ), and it failed to converge on three of the longer tables. Changing the shape of the item curve while keeping one dimension buys a little on some tables and loses more on others, which is not where the predictable signal is either. This is the second time the warehouse has returned that answer. The [asymmetric IRT vignette](asymmetric_irt.qmd) takes the three asymmetric models of @shimbonifay2026 --- the LPE among them --- across dozens of binary IRW tables and scores them on held-out responses with the same IMV. The plain 2PL wins outright on the largest share of tables, and the single best case in that batch is worth about what a typical 1PL-to-2PL upgrade is worth. That page and this one share a measure and a warehouse but not an implementation, a model set or a table list, which makes the agreement worth something. It also reports a thing we cannot see from here: the asymmetric model that looks dominant in-sample by BIC is the weakest of the three once it is scored out of sample. Taken with the previous section, the picture is fairly simple: on dichotomous tables, the 2PL's logistic curve is good enough, and the only thing worth adding is a dimension, when the instrument has one to add. ### Away from the hand-picked tables, the median table gains nothing Twenty-four tables chosen to span kinds of structure cannot tell us how often a second dimension pays. For that we need a rule rather than a judgment, so we applied one to the whole warehouse: dichotomous, at least 500 respondents, at least 10 items, and density at least 0.9, which is what the cell-level split needs. That gives 262 tables, of which 242 fit without incident. The obvious thing to test is whether they carry real structure beyond the first dimension — and the obvious way to test it is a trap we fell into. Correlating the MIRT loadings with the 2PL slopes and taking the better-aligned of the two dimensions produces a correlation with IMV of +0.59, which looks like a finding and is an artifact: MIRT's first dimension recovers the 2PL direction *by construction*, so the statistic is largely measuring how well the fit converged. The repair is to orient the solution before measuring it. Rotate the loading matrix so that its first column lies along the 2PL slope vector, which is permitted because the two-dimensional solution is identified only up to rotation, and then look at what is left in the orthogonal column. That column is the structure a second dimension adds that the 2PL could not already express. Oriented this way, the alignment correlates +0.17 with IMV, and the share of loading variance in the orthogonal column correlates +0.09 — with no monotone pattern across its quartiles. There is no evidence here that extra dimensional structure is what pays. What does pay is cruder. Some IRW tables contain reverse-keyed items that were never recoded; the warehouse does not harmonise the direction of responses, and the 2PL handles such an item by giving it a negative slope, which is a legitimate fit but leaves a mixed-sign slope vector. Reverse keying is the best single predictor we have of where a second dimension pays; it is not the whole of it. This reads as a method factor rather than a dimension of the construct. When a third of an inventory is worded in the opposite direction, a one-dimensional model must choose a single ordering of persons and eat the misfit on the reversed items; a second dimension gives it somewhere to put them. Whether to call that a second substantive dimension or an artifact of wording is a real question, and it is partly a question about the data rather than the model: a table whose reverse-keyed items had been recoded at ingest would show less of it. Readers tempted to read a high IMV here as evidence of a second trait should check the sign of the slopes first. It also qualifies, rather than overturns, Part I. The claim that the gains cluster in personality and clinical inventories survives too — those are exactly the instruments that mix keying directions. What changes is the interpretation: the second dimension those tables need is doing less interesting work than the phrase "multidimensionality" suggests. ### The mirt 2PL gap is an estimator effect, and it is largest on short tests The same 2PL fit by marginal maximum likelihood beats the gradient-descent fit by 0.03 on the 25-item COVID knowledge test, by 0.009 on the 30-item ENCCEJA form and the 18-item financial literacy test, and by nothing on the 116-item residency exam. The Denver screener, with 105 items, looks like an exception until one remembers it is age-adaptive: each child answers only the items near their age, about thirty in training, so it is a short test in the sense that matters. Plotting the gap against the number of training responses each person contributes makes the pattern plain. ::: {#cell-fig-gap .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Estimator gap against test length"} gap = imv_tab["mirt_2pl"] n_resp = pd.Series({t: float(data[t][~data[t].test].groupby("pid").size().median()) for t in gap.index}) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.6)) ax.scatter(n_resp, gap, s=28, color=[group_colour[GROUP_OF[t]] for t in gap.index]) for t in gap.index: if gap[t] > 0.008: ax.annotate(SHORT[t], (n_resp[t], gap[t]), fontsize=7, xytext=(4, 2), textcoords="offset points") ax.axhline(0, color="0.3", lw=0.8) ax.set(xlabel="median training responses per person", ylabel="IMV of mirt 2PL over PyTorch 2PL") ax.grid(color="0.9", lw=0.6); ax.set_axisbelow(True) for sp in ("top", "right"): ax.spines[sp].set_visible(False) plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](nn_irt_files/figure-html/fig-gap-output-1.png){#fig-gap width=649 height=385} ::: ::: Why does it happen? The networks here treat each person's $\theta$ as a parameter to be estimated, and the item parameters are then fit around those point estimates. With a dozen or twenty responses per person those estimates are poor, and the item parameters inherit the error, which is the incidental-parameter problem; `mirt` integrates the persons out instead. That is a story about the estimator rather than the model, and it is worth more than a paragraph, so [Part II](#part-ii) takes it apart. We have left the network as it is so that the effect stays visible here: it is the price of the simplest possible estimator, and readers who build their own networks should know it is there. # Part II. Estimation: which estimator closes the gap to mirt? {#part-ii} ## What Part I could not separate Two things differ between the torch 2PL and the `mirt` 2PL, and Part I could not separate them. One is how the scale of the person parameters is set: the PyTorch 2PL puts a penalty on $\theta$, while `mirt` fixes its population variance by assumption. The other is the estimator: the PyTorch model is fit by gradient descent on the joint likelihood, with each person's $\theta$ treated as a parameter, while `mirt` integrates the persons out. Part II separates the two. Every estimator below is fit to the same training cells and scored on the same held-out cells, and each is compared with `mirt` by the InterModel Vigorish. ## The estimators Each estimator is a different way of fitting the same 2PL, $\operatorname{logit} P(y_{pi}=1) = a_i\theta_p + d_i$. Two of them come from the prior-or-constraint choice for the scale, and two from the estimator choice. - **Adam, prior.** Minibatch gradient descent on the joint log-likelihood plus an $N(0,1)$ penalty on each $\theta_p$, stopped at the best held-out epoch. This is the network used throughout Part I. - **Adam, constrained.** The same network with $\theta$ standardised across persons in the forward pass, so it has mean zero and SD one by construction, and no penalty. - **Alternating JML, prior.** Joint maximum likelihood by block updates: with the items fixed, a Newton step for every person's $\theta_p$ (with the $N(0,1)$ penalty, so this is alternating MAP); with the persons fixed, a Newton step for every item's $(a_i, d_i)$. Repeat. - **Alternating JML, constrained.** The same block updates without the penalty. After each person update $\theta$ is standardised, and the scale is moved into $a$ and $d$, which leaves the fitted probabilities unchanged. - **EM, marginal maximum likelihood.** The estimator `mirt` uses. The E-step gives each person a posterior over a quadrature grid, given their training cells; the M-step fits each item's $(a_i, d_i)$ by weighted logistic regression on the grid. Held-out cells get the posterior-predictive probability. - **MML, L-BFGS.** Start from 200 EM iterations, then maximise the marginal likelihood directly with `torch.optim.LBFGS` and autograd. Same model and objective as EM; a different optimiser for the last step. Joint and alternating estimators predict with the point estimates of $\theta_p$ (plug-in). EM and MML predict with the posterior. The Adam networks stop at their best held-out epoch, and the alternating JML fits stop at their best held-out sweep, which is the same rule and the same caveat: the held-out set also picks the stopping point. ## The scale is fixed weakly by the penalty The prior version fixes the scale of $\theta$ only through the penalty. In the likelihood $a_i\theta_p$ is the only thing that matters, so the same fit can be written with a small $\theta$ and a large $a$, and the penalty pulls $\theta$ toward zero at a constant price. Alternating JML makes the drift easy to see. The run below uses no early stopping and records the person SD and the median slope every 100 sweeps on the residency exam. ::: {#cell-fig-drift .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Scale drift in the prior version of alternating JML"} drift = pd.read_csv(DATA / "drift_borges_alt_jml.csv") fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.6)) ax[0].plot(drift.sweep, drift.theta_sd, color="#2a78d6") ax[0].set(xlabel="sweep", ylabel=r"SD of $\hat\theta$", title="person SD") ax[1].plot(drift.sweep, drift.median_a, color="#eb6834") ax[1].set(xlabel="sweep", ylabel="median slope $a$", title="item slopes") for a_ in ax: for sp in ("top", "right"): a_.spines[sp].set_visible(False) plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() print(drift.iloc[[0, 1, 5, 10, -1]].round(4).to_string(index=False)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](nn_irt_files/figure-html/fig-drift-output-1.png){#fig-drift width=975 height=385} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` sweep theta_sd median_a heldout_logloss 1 0.5458 1.0593 0.5504 100 0.1799 3.2187 0.5482 500 0.0850 6.8346 0.5482 1000 0.0611 9.5222 0.5482 2000 0.0438 13.2753 0.5482 ``` ::: ::: Over 2000 sweeps the person SD falls from 0.55 to 0.04 and the median slope rises from 1.1 to 13. With the Rasch model written the usual way --- $\theta_p + d_i$, no slope --- the constraint was catastrophic: worse on every one of the 24 tables, by 0.03 on average and by 0.19 on the Onah test. That is not what it costs to fix the scale. It is what it costs to fix the scale with nothing left to absorb it. The prior version lets the data set the spread of $\theta$, which comes out at 0.56 on the residency exam and 0.40 on the Onah test, and the slopeless Rasch has no way to express that the spread should not be one. Giving it a single slope $c$ shared by every item --- still a Rasch model, since the items continue to differ only in difficulty --- removes the problem entirely: the constrained Rasch is then within 0.0001 of the prior version on average and ahead of it on half the tables. The lesson is about identification, not about the constraint: a model that cannot represent the scale should not be asked to fix it. With that repaired, the cost of the constraint is small and consistent across the five networks: $-0.0017$ for the 2PL, $-0.0021$ for the MIRT, $-0.0030$ and $-0.0028$ for the two MLPs, and $+0.0001$ for the Rasch. It is also concentrated where theory says it should be. On tests where people answer many items the constraint is free or slightly positive; on short tests every model pays, with the worst single losses on the ASQ (17 training responses per person) and the Ding knowledge test (19). Standardising $\theta$ divides out the spread of estimates that are mostly noise on a short test, which stretches poorly determined person parameters back to a spread of one instead of shrinking them toward zero. That is the same incidental-parameter story as above, seen from the other side. The constraint does not stop the wide networks from overfitting, either. So fixing the scale changes how the scale is set, not whether the wide networks memorise their training cells, and early stopping is still what keeps them honest. # Limitations ## Of the model comparison - **The held-out set is also the validation set.** Each PyTorch model is reported at its best held-out epoch, which flatters every network by a small amount and the wider ones by slightly more, since they have more epochs at which to get lucky. A third split would fix this; we judged that at 24 tables and five models the bias is small relative to the effects reported, and the direction is known: it works against the 2PL, not for it. Note that the same practice tilts Part II the other way. There the networks and the alternating JML fits stop on the held-out cells while `mirt` never sees them, so the estimator gap reported there is if anything an underestimate. In both parts the thumb is on the networks' side. - **Two estimators, one model.** The PyTorch 2PL (MAP by gradient descent) and the `mirt` 2PL (marginal maximum likelihood) are the same model and do not give the same held-out loss. The comparison that is fair is therefore networks against the PyTorch 2PL and flexible curves against the `mirt` 2PL, and Part I is written that way. Part II shows that an estimator which integrates over the persons closes the gap in torch, and that fixing the scale of $\theta$ does not. - **Only person and item identities enter the model.** The networks see exactly what the classical models see, so this is a comparison of functional forms, not of information. Sequential models of learning [@piech2015dkt] use the order of responses; models with item text as input can predict items never seen in training; variational IRT replaces the point estimates with an encoder network. All of these use more than the (person, item, response) triple, and all can be scored with the same held-out cells and the same IMV, but none is on this page. - **Dichotomous, dense tables only.** The cell-level split and the Bernoulli loss are written for 0/1 responses. Polytomous tables need a different output layer and a different loss; sparse tables raise the question of whether the missingness is informative. - **Subsampling.** Tables are capped at 5,000 respondents and 116 items. The gains reported for the inventories are therefore gains at that size; a wider network may do relatively better with more data, which is the usual pattern and is not tested here. - **Twenty-four tables, chosen by hand.** The groups were picked to span kinds of structure, not sampled from the warehouse, and the counts per group are small. The qualitative pattern (dimension helps where there is one, depth does not) is consistent across the groups; the sizes of the gains are specific to these tables, and the sweep confirms that the set is enriched — roughly double the corpus rate of gains above 0.005. - **The sweep is narrower than the comparison it generalises.** The 242-table sweep fits the 2PL against a two-dimensional MIRT and nothing else. It can say how often the one move that worked in Part I pays, and it can say what the paying tables have in common, but it says nothing about depth, about flexible item curves, or about the estimator gap — all of which rest on the 24 tables alone. Its selection rule also caps fetched tables at two million responses, which excludes the largest mass administrations (the million-respondent ENEM forms among them), and its density threshold of 0.9 excludes adaptive instruments, including two of Part I's own tables. - **The sweep treats tables as independent, and the warehouse does not.** IRW holds several tables from some deposits, and two of them sit among the largest gains in the sweep (`vogel_2024_citizen_attributes_s2` and `_s3`, at +0.094 and +0.091). Nothing in the selection rule or the summaries accounts for that, so the tail is less varied than a count of 242 suggests, and any standard error computed as though those tables were independent would be too small. We report no such standard error for that reason. - **Keying is measured, not established.** The fraction of items with a negative fitted 2PL slope is a symptom of reverse-keyed items that were not recoded, but it is not a direct observation of the item wording. A negative slope can also mean a mis-scored key, a badly behaved item, or a genuinely oppositional trait. We did not read the items; a table-by-table check of wording against slope sign would settle it and is not on this page. ## Of the estimator comparison - **Two estimators are on a common footing; the networks are not.** The MML fits are the same model as `mirt` and are compared directly. The Adam networks and the alternating JML fits are different estimators of the same model, and their gaps to `mirt` are gaps in estimation, not in the model. - **Stopping uses the held-out set.** The Adam networks and both alternating JML fits pick their stopping point on the held-out cells, which flatters them slightly. The MML fits do not use held-out data at all: they maximise the training likelihood (EM, then four L-BFGS rounds). - **Items with extreme parameters.** On the ASQ, Denver and EDSC screeners several items have parameters in the hundreds, and the marginal likelihood is flat along them. Two correct maximisers can stop at different points there, which is why the largest MML disagreements with `mirt` are on those tables. - **Dichotomous 2PL only.** The estimators here are for the 2PL on 0/1 responses, and the multidimensional and nonlinear networks are not refit with them. # Reproducibility **Source code for this page:** [`nn_irt.qmd`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt.qmd), [`nn_irt_helpers.py`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_helpers.py), [`nn_irt_chart.py`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_chart.py), [`nn_irt_mirt_compute.R`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_mirt_compute.R), and, for Part II, [`nn_irt_estimation.py`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_estimation.py), [`nn_irt_estimation_compute.py`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_estimation_compute.py) and [`nn_irt_estimation_drift.py`](https://github.com/datapages/irw/blob/main/vignettes/nn_irt_estimation_drift.py).
